text: Before the fleet there are drawings: Lee Sun-shin is designing and building the Turtle Ships while the invasion he expects is still only expected. A hundred and twenty-five minutes leaves room for a film to care about preparation as much as battle, and Jang Il-ho takes the Injin War from the side of the man who has to think about hulls and plating before anyone fires. The court is the second front. Victories at sea raise him, and the same victories make him a name in military circles, which is the one quality a nervous king cannot afford to admire in a subject. The Grand Bell Award named it the best Korean film of 1977. Its most sustained interest is not the water but the palace, where a man's usefulness and his danger turn out to be the same fact about him.

Area 598 is a map reference before it is a fortress, and the soldiers sent to destroy it are handed the arithmetic along with the order. The operation is planned around losses, and the men carrying it out know about the planning. That removes the usual suspense and replaces it with something harder to shoot: how people conduct themselves in the interval between accepting terms and meeting them. Lee Won-se directed it in 1978, a quarter century after the fighting, and the Baeksang Arts Awards named it that year's best film. The Korean War picture made in Korea carries a complication no other war film has to solve, which is that the enemy territory the unit walks into is not foreign ground, and the deeper they go the closer they get to home.

Chun-sam works Bong-pil's land for no wages on the understanding that he is marrying into the family, and Bong-pil keeps discovering that his daughter has not finished growing. Jeom-sun has finished growing. The arrangement is a labour contract wearing an engagement's clothes, and the father has an obvious interest in postponing a wedding for as long as his prospective son-in-law will accept postponement. Sixty-five minutes gives Kim Soo-yong no room for a subplot and he does not appear to want one: three people, one farm, and a comedy that runs on who is willing to stop working. What is being negotiated is not romance but labour, the price of a grown daughter paid in years. The wedding that keeps not happening is a way of paying nobody.

A detective is trying to establish how a young man died, and the trail runs through prostitution and through faith with the same patience. Yu Hyun-mok uses the shape of an investigation to pursue a question no investigation can close, which is what the dead man believed and whether believing it had anything to do with what became of him. Detection suits that job because it is procedural and obstinate, and because a detective is obliged to keep asking after everyone else has agreed on an answer. A hundred and ten minutes, 1980, the Grand Bell Award for best film. The religious material is not scenery: one man works with evidence and testimony, and the explanations he keeps meeting belong to a different order of authority entirely.

Two later filmmakers thought the material worth shooting again, which is a verdict of sorts on a comedy from 1926. Yutaka Abe sets a writer against a woman who steals, and the pairing carries the joke: one of them invents for a living, the other needs to be believed exactly once. Seventy-seven minutes, made in Japan in the mid-twenties, so the humour has to survive in gesture, in timing, in where a hand goes and how long it stays, rather than in anything an audience can hear. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of its year. A premise filmed three times has a mechanism in it, and the mechanism here is an encounter between two kinds of professional dishonesty. Irony is the word that came down attached to this one, and irony in a story about theft usually means the film declines to be as scandalised by the thief as the writer is.

A hundred and forty-five minutes is a great deal of film for one physician's career, and the length is the argument. The life of Heo Jun proceeds by increments: a teacher outgrown, a rank conferred, a patient of higher standing than the last. He starts as a low-level politician's son and arrives at the king's own body, which in a court is the object the entire arrangement is built around. The nobles who resent him are not a subplot. A man promoted past his birth is a standing problem for anyone whose position depends on birth staying decisive, and the plots against him are that problem taking practical form. Choi In-hyeon directed it in 1976. Medicine here is a skill, a service, and a way through a wall that was not built with doors.

Nan-hee is a college student, and her boyfriend is teaching her, patiently, how to kill a man. The move into the work is gradual, coercion arriving in the shape of a relationship with lessons in it, and the target chosen for her is the officer who runs the investigative unit named in the title. Seol Tae-ho shot this in 1973 at ninety-one minutes, and the compression tells: the preparing and the approaching sit almost side by side, so the person she has been assembled into is never far from the student she was a season earlier. The Baeksang Arts Awards named it the best film of its year. Crime pictures usually place the moral difficulty after the act, in the aftermath where guilt is cheap. This one puts it in the training, where there is nothing yet to regret.

Crop circles and cathedrals are filed under the same heading here, and the filing is the argument rather than an aside. Freddy Silva's fifty-four minutes move among British sites, Stonehenge among them, on the premise that the people who raised them were engineers of a spiritual technology, building for a measurable effect on whoever stands inside. The method is not laboratory work. It is walking: stone, site, the shape of a place, one after another until the pattern begins to feel like intention. A viewer who grants none of it can still watch the appetite at work, and the appetite is the interesting part, since what is being proposed is that the oldest structures in the country are instruments and the instructions are still legible in the masonry.

The throne passes to King Ko-jang, judged too inexperienced to use it, so his uncle governs in his name. It is the sort of arrangement everyone can call temporary because nobody has to set a date. Shin Sang-ok puts the regent opposite Queen Min, whose political intelligence is the film's motor, and the contest is fought in the only rooms available to it: a court, a household, a marriage. Min is the young king's wife, which makes the fight domestic before it is political, since the regent is family and so is the person contesting him. Two hours, 1968, the Grand Bell Award for best film. A regency is a legal fiction with a person inside it, power exercised on behalf of a boy who is present in the building, growing every year, and watching the man who holds it do the holding.

A crate of counterfeit watches, shipped in from Hong Kong, is the kind of case that ought to close in a week. The policeman who opens it is himself an immigrant, and following the consignment means following his own route backwards, until the file stops being about merchandise at all. Fakes make a good centre for a story like this: the object is a thing pretending to be a thing, sold to buyers who are purchasing the look and know the price of the look. Luk Chi-Gong keeps the register of drama rather than chase, which is the right choice for a case whose difficulty is not physical. The pressure falls on a man whose work requires distance from a place he came out of, and whose investigation keeps shortening that distance.
